piezas.titulo: Towards Robust Vision-Language Reasoning: A Multi-Stage Optimization Pipeline with Masked Diffusion Model
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.15238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.

piezas.titulo: The open AI-native stack on Kubernetes: From open models to distributed inference and agents
piezas.resumenOriginal:
Over the past decade, Kubernetes established itself as the standard for orchestrating microservices and containerized applications. Today, we're witnessing the next major architectural shift in distributed computing: AI workloads moving from isolated research prototypes into large-scale, multi-tenant production fleets . In this post, we'll walk through the open-source stack that powers this shift and show you the sample manifests that you can try on your own Kubernetes clusters. You can also join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 to see these projects in action through live demos and technical sessions. For modern engineering teams, production AI is rapidly moving beyond generic calls to closed, black-box APIs. Organizations are realizing that their long-term competitive advantage lies in domain specialization. Platform engineers, ML researchers, and AI builders want the autonomy to run high-performing open-weight models (such as the Gemma family). They want to adapt them to proprietary enterprise datasets by using reinforcement learning (RL) and serve them with predictable latency, high throughput, and maximum hardware efficiency. Whether it's scientific initiatives training domain models like DolphinGemma (an LLM helping scientists study how dolphins communicate) on acoustic data, legal platforms evaluating complex contracts, or engineering teams building autonomous coding agents, the objective is the same: achieving frontier-level task performance at a fraction of the serving cost and latency. Yet, scaling RL post-training, stateful distributed inference, and autonomous agent execution on traditional container infrastructure introduces substantial hurdles: Accelerator underutilization in RL : When you alternate between training and rollout generation, expensive GPUs and TPUs remain idle for most of the training run. Cache-blind load balancing : When you use standard Kubernetes round-robin and least-connections routing, multi-turn agent calls are scattered across arbitrary pods and wipe out key-value (KV) cache locality. Framework fragmentation : When you operate parallel, siloed compute clusters (such as bespoke Ray or Slurm setups) alongside Kubernetes, you fragment capacity and multiply maintenance toil. Agent security in multi-tenant clusters: When you execute untrusted, model-generated shell commands and scripts in shared environments, you expose clusters to sandbox escapes and privilege escalation. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 , Google Cloud is addressing these challenges by introducing and expanding a unified, open-source AI-native stack across Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) based on these components: OpenRL (CNCF Sandbox): A Kubernetes-native post training service that simplifies RL post-training and maximizes accelerator utilization. llm-d 1.0 (CNCF Sandbox): An open distributed inference control plane that provides prefix-cache-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and multi-tier KV cache management. Ray on GKE with KubeRay (CNCF Sandbox) : A framework that provides enterprise lifecycle management, elastic autoscaling, and Kueue -driven scheduling for distributed Ray compute and data processing. Agent Substrate (CNCF Sandbox) : An open orchestration runtime that provides lifecycle management and execution targets for multi-turn AI agent workflows. gVisor (CNCF Sandbox) : A kernel-level container sandbox that delivers strong system call isolation when you execute untrusted agent code in multi-tenant clusters. TorchTPU : A backend that provides first-class, native PyTorch support across Cloud TPUs and GPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang . Bridge reinforcement learning and Kubernetes with OpenRL While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice, domain excellence especially in multi-step reasoning, mathematical proofing, and autonomous tool use requires RL. Historically, it's been difficult to bridge the world of ML experimentation with production Kubernetes fleets. ML researchers want to iterate rapidly in Python and PyTorch by using standard reward functions, while platform teams need multi-tenant governance, quota enforcement, and predictable scheduling. To eliminate this friction, Google created OpenRL and contributed it to the CNCF Sandbox . Architectural highlights of OpenRL Clean 4-primitive Python abstraction : Researchers write standard Python training code that's centered around four core primitives ( forward_backward , optim_step , sample , and save_state ). OpenRL translates these primitives into Kubernetes scheduling workflows without requiring developers to learn Kubernetes internals or manage infrastructure code. Cooperative accelerator time-slicing : OpenRL interleaves training steps and rollout inferences on the same physical accelerators. This approach avoids the need to dedicate separate, static clusters to compute-bound training and latency-sensitive rollout generation. Delta-weight synchronization : Shipping full multi-gigabyte model weights over cluster networking after every optimization step creates massive network saturation. OpenRL transmits only parameter deltas to rollout workers, eliminating rollout cold starts. Zero-config dynamic resource allocation ( DRA ) : OpenRL automatically profiles model context lengths, batch dimensions, and LoRA versus full fine-tuning configurations. It then dynamically bin-packs workloads across a heterogenous accelerator fleet by using native Kubernetes DRA claims. Distributed inference at scale with llm-d 1.0 After you post-train a model, serving it serving it under interactive, bursty agent traffic presents a new set of distributed systems challenges. Standard ingress controllers treat LLM traffic as stateless HTTP requests, scattering sequential turns across different replicas and constantly rebuilding KV cache. Google Cloud, Red Hat, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA co-founded the project, with contributions from over 500 engineers across 25+ organizations. Today, llm-d 1.0 is the CNCF Sandbox distributed inference control plane that transforms standalone inference engines (like vLLM and SGLang) into a coordinated, cluster-wide serving fabric. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: inference.networking.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1

The Endpoint Picker evaluates real-time KV cache residency across worker pods. In production deployments, it's doubled KV cache hit rates from 35% to 70% and cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 70-85% on multi-turn agent workloads. 3-Tier KV cache offload : When accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM) nears capacity during long-context interactions, llm-d cascades KV cache blocks from HBM → host CPU RAM → local NVMe SSD / Google Cloud Managed Lustre / Cloud Storage. This offload prevents expensive context recalculations. DisaggregatedSet is built built on Kubernetes LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) . It enables independent horizontal scaling and coordinated, zero-downtime rolling upgrades. Latency-tolerant async processing & flow control : The llm-d-async-processor component pulls background, latency-tolerant tasks from Pub/Sub or Redis into cluster slack capacity. It applies strict traffic prioritization so background processing never degrades interactive user experiences. Fleet observability with Prism : Track cluster-wide throughput, inter-token latency (ITL), TTFT, and cache hit ratios by using Prism , the llm-d open-source benchmarking and performance dashboard. Native Kueue queueing & multi-tenancy : KubeRay integrates directly with Kueue for multi-tenant fair sharing, priority preemption, and quota management across shared GPU and TPU capacity. Elastic autoscaling : KubeRay dynamically scales worker pods based on active Ray tasks and actor placement, preventing idle resource consumption. Strong isolation for AI agents: Agent Substrate & gVisor As multi-turn AI agents advance from conversational assistants to autonomous systems that generate code, execute shell commands, and orchestrate external APIs running untrusted, model-generated code in shared clusters introduces serious security risks. Google Cloud is contributing Agent Substrate and continuing core contributions to gVisor in the CNCF Sandbox: Kernel-level sandboxing : gVisor provides a user-space kernel that intercepts and virtualizes system calls, which helps ensure that untrusted agent code can't compromise the host kernel or access neighboring tenant workloads. Sub-second ephemeral execution : Sandboxes spin up in milliseconds per agent turn, providing isolated execution environments for both RL rollout generation in OpenRL and live production agent workflows. Proven in practice: Mastering domain reasoning To evaluate this complete open-source stack on a rigorous enterprise workload, we tested Gemma 4 against the open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) developed by Harvey.ai . piezas.titulo: Occupational Therapy in LGBTQ + Affirming Primary Care: Referral, Intervention, and Outcomes.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceLGBTQ + clients experience healthcare barriers that may shape daily routines, health management, and participation. Little is known about occupational therapy referral pathways and outcomes in LGBTQ + affirming primary care.ObjectiveTo describe referral characteristics, occupational performance concerns, intervention focus, and client-reported outcomes among LGBTQ + clients referred to occupational therapy.DesignRetrospective pilot program evaluation using clinical documentation and outcome data from July 2025 through March 2026, with a June 2026 analysis cutoff.SettingTwo Midwestern primary care settings where occupational therapy screening and referral processes were developed; ongoing intervention occurred through outpatient occupational therapy.ParticipantsThirty-nine referred clients were included in descriptive analyses; 38 received intervention beyond evaluation; 21 had complete baseline and follow-up Canadian Occupational Performance Measure data.InterventionIndividualized outpatient occupational therapy focused on client-identified concerns.Outcomes and MeasuresReferral and treatment characteristics, occupational performance concerns, coded occupational focus, and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure Performance and Satisfaction ratings.ResultsCommon concerns included instrumental activities of daily living (94.9%), health management/self-management (92.3%), activities of daily living (82.1%), and work or school participation (82.1%). The most common primary intervention focus was health management and chronic condition self-management (65.8%). Among participants with outcome data, COPM Performance scores improved by 2.29 points and Satisfaction scores improved by 2.58 points.Conclusions and RelevanceOccupational therapy may support LGBTQ + clients referred from primary care by addressing needs related to health management, routines, self-care, and participation through individualized outpatient intervention. Prospective multisite research is needed.

piezas.titulo: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
piezas.resumenOriginal: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious. I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access ’s required style. At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed. What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.” Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too. Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself. ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI 1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field. 2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections. 3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.” 4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access . 5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access , where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. → CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. ROUND 2: FARS 1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes. 2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal. 3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete. 4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article. 5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access . → CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints. Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job? As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini! In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub , she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong ” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.” Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto , an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable. The AI Arms Race On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making. These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi , IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through. Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics. Burden on Academics Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop. Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers Round 1: The Fake Paper Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini Ghost citations Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated. Questionable scientific claims An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable. Too many acronyms The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract. Round 2: The AI-Research Paper Created by the autonomous research system FARS Too many preprints The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints. Nonsense in a figure One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.” AI artifacts Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots. There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record. Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky , cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles. Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.” Blurred Lines My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System) , AutoResearchClaw , The AIScientist-v2 , Zochi , AI Researcher , and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw , for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery. The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.” FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours , was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma . “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su , Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.) Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test. Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously. Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time. With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours. At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney. Round 2: Attempt to Publish Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one. “Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem. In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated. Automation Changing the Landscape Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process. “FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge ,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.” In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?” A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future? Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.” In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?” To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’” Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent. Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

piezas.titulo: Employment in Veterans With Mental Illness: An Exploratory Penalized-Regression and Random-Forest Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceReturning to civilian and community life after military service represents a critical and often challenging transition. Employment can contribute to social identity, financial security, social participation and community reintegration, and overall quality of life among veterans.ObjectiveTo examine candidate factors of employment among veterans who reported a current mental health diagnosis.DesignCross-sectional survey study.SettingOnline data collection.ParticipantsA total of 156 veterans who reported having a current mental illness were recruited; 151 with complete data (mean age = 37.85 years) were analyzed. Most participants identified as male (67%), White (70%), and married or living with a partner (62%).Outcomes and MeasuresEmployment status was the outcome, and candidate predictors included demographic and military characteristics, mental health, physical health and functioning, and psychosocial and behavioral factors.ResultsThe BIC-LASSO model revealed that greater disability severity and pain intensity were each associated with lower odds of employment, with moderate bootstrap selection recurrence (57.1% for disability severity and 56.9% for pain intensity) that remained robust after sensitivity analysis. The random forest model did not exceed majority-class accuracy.Conclusions and RelevanceGreater disability severity and greater pain intensity emerged as plausible, though not yet confirmed, correlates of employment status among veterans with mental illness. Because these exploratory findings require replication in larger, more diverse, and longitudinal samples, they do not yet justify changes to practice; in the interim, they support attending to everyday functioning and pain, alongside psychiatric symptoms, when occupational therapy practitioners evaluate work participation with this population.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: November 10
piezas.resumenOriginal: It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends . One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on? Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on the recent election’s impact on data centers . I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI: you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition. He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming. There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments. To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse . He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering , in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is . I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data? His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming . Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. While we don’t know if we’ll ever be able to download skills directly into our brains ( “I know kung fu” - or for those in my particular demographic: Joe 90 ), this does raise the possibility of downloading capabilities into models by manipulating their weights. Simon Wilison riffed on this paper by examining whether an LLM can understand model behaviors from the weights alone , by examining four simple neural networks, each trained to play a specific game, and figuring out which game it was by just looking at the weights. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Jessica Kerr (jessitron): My days of teaching AI to do stuff are numbered. Getting it to teach me stuff is more fun. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Houck et al (that “al” includes some folks who I’ve learned to pay a lot of attention to), look at how we can assess the quality of context supplied to agents. An agent may draw from source code, specifications, issue trackers, chat histories, architectural documents, tool output, and user instructions, then act on that combination with limited human supervision. Information that was written for different audiences, at different times, and for different purposes is brought together into a temporary operating environment for a particular task. Whether each source is individually useful does not reveal whether the resulting context is fit for the work the agent is being asked to do. They’ve come up with a framework for describing the quality of this assembled context , which they refer to as CAFE(S). The acronym refers to five dimensions they look at: Clarity: Can the agent interpret the request as intended? Actionability: Can the agent proceed, and know when it is done? Fidelity: Can the agent trust that this context is true? Efficiency: Can the agent focus on what matters? Security: Should the agent have this context at all? They also list a set of half-a-dozen “context smells”: common cases where these break down (and a nod to Kent’s original metaphor ) I’m not sure about the name, (how exactly should I pronounce “CAFE(S)”?) and the article exhibits rather more LLM Voice that I prefer. But on the whole I think this is a good framing for thinking about an important part of feeding our silicon servants/overlords. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Cindy Sridharan noted that the problems she ran into six months ago are no longer around : What was missing in my setup 6 months ago was the verification process I now use. 70% of my daily token spend goes into verifying patches, and only ~20-30% into creating them. That resonated with conversations I’ve had with folks using agents in enterprise settings. They are using far more tokens to check the working of models (through guardrails and evals) than they are to generate a response to a request. A single request to a model from a customer may trigger a dozen turns to other models to probe its input and verify its output.

piezas.titulo: Detecting Duplicates With Machine Learning in 2026: From String Metrics to Embeddings and LLMs
piezas.resumenOriginal: The more data companies gather on their customers, products, and code, the more duplicated information accumulates, confusing the teams who depend on it. You don't go through millions of records manually. So deduplication is now a machine learning problem. This article looks at the current state of duplicate detection in ML systems where the old techniques still work, and what embeddings and large language models have brought to the table. How Do ML Systems Detect Duplicates? It is possible for a person to look at two pictures or two strings and know if they are the same. Teaching a machine to do the same raises difficult questions. What is 'like'? There are degrees of resemblance. Is “Jon Smith, 12 Oak St.” the same customer as “Jonathan Smith, 12 Oak Street?”

Each night, STAR's Clinical Director will be joined by a different STAR therapist to share tips and strategies around some of families' most often asked questions including: “How can I support and be there for my family when I am constantly feeling burned out?” “What can I do to help my child transition from thing to thing/place to place more smoothly?" “We feel like we walk on egg shells around our child. As a social worker, she provided case management, program development, and program management. Mim has taught both university level (California State-Dominguez Hills) and professional continuing education courses since 2013, spoken internationally, and has co-authored works for professional publications. She has been in her current role at STAR Institute since 2017 at the invitation of Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, PhD, FAOTA, OTR. Gina’s practice is rooted in attachment and systems theories, making her truly a relationally focused therapist. As such, she believes that our greatest healing occurs in the context of relationships. She has always been oriented toward a biopsychosocial approach to her theory of change, thereby honoring the importance of the mind-body connection. She believes that within a safe space and through our attuned relationship with Self and others, we all have the power to tune into our instinct towards healing. With her early career in occupational therapy, Gina has incredible understanding of the importance of self-determination for clients: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. This—coupled with her deep understanding of sensory integration and processing and the importance of occupational roles—truly sets her apart. Her practice honors and respects each person’s unique history and individual differences, and sets clients up for experiencing a deeper sense of self and relational health, on the clients’ own terms. Gina was drawn to couples and family therapy for its non-pathologizing approach to viewing clients’ problems. While biological factors certainly play a role, so do clients’ experiences within their families, partnerships, and larger society. She is passionate about empowering parents to reflect on and integrate their own experiences in service of their children’s health and wellness, as well as their own. “Society does not prioritize proactively supporting its members’ health and therefore, parents and families are not set up for success. Gina is especially equipped to support neurodivergent individuals, couples and families, as well as those navigating issues around disability and chronic illness. She is capable of easily moving between deep therapeutic work, parent coaching and individual skills training - making her a versatile therapist. She has experience supporting clients with life transitions, anxiety, depression, non-suicidal self-harm, suicidal ideation, recovery from adverse childhood experiences and trauma, developing deeper emotional awareness, identifying and leaving behind maladaptive coping patterns, and improving self-esteem. Above all, Gina is a sensory informed, neurodiversity affirming and LGBTQIA+ allied, culturally sensitive and attachment-focused therapist with a special interest in interpersonal neurobiology who strongly believes in the healing power of making sense of our experiences in the context of relationships where we feel seen, heard, and understood. piezas.titulo: Postcentral cortical thickness reduction in trigeminal neuralgia: a whole-brain surface-based morphometry MRI study
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionTrigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a neuropathic pain disorder characterized by paroxysmal unilateral facial pain evoked by innocuous cutaneous stimulation or manoeuvres. In classical and idiopathic TN, objective evidence of somatosensory system damage is often difficult to demonstrate. Neuroimaging studies suggest cortical structural alterations, though findings have been inconsistent, likely reflecting variability in case definitions and cortical measurement methodologies. We therefore investigated cortical thickness changes in a biologically homogeneous cohort of patients with right-sided TN using a whole-brain surface-based morphometry (SBM) approach.Methods60 patients with classical or idiopathic right-sided TN and 30 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent 3 T structural MRI. Cortical thickness was computed using FreeSurfer. Whole-brain vertex-wise group comparisons were performed using a General Linear Model (GLM) with a non-parametric permutation-based cluster-wise correction for multiple comparisons.ResultsCompared with controls, patients with TN showed significantly reduced cortical thickness in eight clusters. The largest and most significant cluster was located in the left postcentral gyrus. Additional clusters were identified in the bilateral insular-temporal regions, the right precentral-postcentral region, the right lateral occipital cortex, and the right parieto-occipital junction. Cortical thickness within significant clusters did not correlate with disease duration.ConclusionRight-sided TN is associated with focal cortical thinning involving both somatosensory and associative cortical regions. While involvement of insular, parietal, and occipital cortices is consistent with network-level structural reorganization observed in chronic pain conditions, thinning of the contralateral postcentral cortex may reflect central changes secondary to damage of primary trigeminal afferents.

piezas.titulo: Neuronal Aralar/AGC1 deficiency impairs social behavior through dopaminergic and redox dysfunction and is rescued by β-hydroxybutyrate
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background: Pathogenic variants in SLC25A12/AGC1 (Aralar) have been linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the mechanisms connecting neuronal metabolic dysfunction to altered social behavior remain poorly understood. Aralar is a key component of the malate-aspartate shuttle, supporting neuronal oxidative metabolism and lactate utilization. Here, we investigated the consequences of postnatal neuronal Aralar deletion and the therapeutic potential of {beta}-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). Methods: We generated neuron-specific Aralar knockout mice (Neu Aralar-KO) using CamKII-Cre, producing efficient recombination in cortex, hippocampus, and striatum. Behavioral, transcriptomic, neurochemical, morphometric, histological, and biochemical analyses were performed in adult mice. The effects of systemic BHB administration were assessed using behavioral, metabolic, oxidative stress, and transcriptomic endpoints. Results: Despite a 55-65% reduction of Aralar expression in forebrain regions, Neu Aralar-KO mice displayed normal growth, survival, brain structure, and myelination. Unexpectedly, loss of neuronal Aralar did not impair spatial memory, episodic memory, or reversal learning. In contrast, Neu Aralar-KO mice exhibited hyperactivity and a marked deficit in sociability, revealing an ASD-relevant behavioral phenotype. Morphological analysis showed significant remodeling of striatal dendritic spines without changes in spine density. Transcriptomic profiling identified 433 differentially expressed genes, the vast majority being upregulated, with enrichment of pathways related to neuropeptide signaling, synaptic transmission, membrane excitability, and behavior. Notably, genes involved in dopamine (DA) and glutamate handling, synaptic connectivity, neuromodulatory signaling, and ASD-associated pathways were strongly induced. Neurochemical analyses revealed preserved glutamate and GABA levels but reduced striatal DA content accompanied by an increased DOPAC/DA ratio, indicating enhanced DA degradation. DAergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) showed minimal recombination, suggesting that DA dysfunction arises through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Consistent with increased DA oxidative catabolism, Neu Aralar-KO striata displayed elevated lipid peroxidation, induction of glutathione-related pathways, upregulation of antioxidant genes, and astrocyte activation. Remarkably, BHB treatment restored sociability, normalized striatal metabolic alterations, reduced oxidative stress, and abolished genotype-dependent neurochemical abnormalities. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed that Aralar deficiency recapitulates a substantial fraction of the fasting/BHB-induced epigenetic transcriptional program. Conclusions: Postnatal neuronal Aralar deficiency uncouples social behavior from cognitive performance and drives ASD-like phenotypes through a mechanism linking neuronal metabolic dysfunction, oxidative stress, glial activation, and impaired DAergic homeostasis. The rescue of behavioral, metabolic, and redox abnormalities by BHB identifies restoration of metabolic homeostasis as a major therapeutic mechanism and highlights metabolic interventions as promising strategies for AGC1 deficiency and ASD-associated disorders involving neuronal metabolic dysfunction.

piezas.titulo: An EMG-driven virtual reality platform for physiology-based motor interaction: technical and functional validation
piezas.resumenOriginal: Harnessing experience-dependent neuroplasticity has become a central goal of modern neurorehabilitation. Immersive virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising tool, enabling task-oriented training in ecologically valid scenarios that are difficult to reproduce in conventional clinical settings. Despite these advances, interaction in most existing VR rehabilitation systems remains primarily mediated by external interfaces, such as motion tracking or handheld controllers, rather than by the user’s own physiological motor activity. Consequently, rehabilitation often fails to directly engage the physiological motor commands that naturally drive voluntary movement. We present and validate an integrated VR–electromyography (VR-EMG) platform that enables closed-loop, physiology-driven interaction between users and immersive virtual environments. The platform combines a standalone VR architecture with wearable EMG systems, online EMG decoding, and cloud-based performance monitoring within a unified framework. A standardized motor-command interface enables different EMG acquisition systems to control both anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic virtual effectors without modifying the decoding strategy or rehabilitation scenarios, providing a flexible framework for diverse applications. The platform was validated through complementary technical and functional evaluations performed on the two supported EMG acquisition systems. Technical validation assessed signal quality, gesture classification accuracy, communication latency, and system reliability. Functional validation was conducted in individuals with upper-limb amputation and able-bodied controls while performing object-interaction tasks across multiple immersive virtual scenarios. The platform demonstrated stable closed-loop operation, reliable gesture recognition, and the ability to quantify objective performance metrics, including task score, completion time, gesture classification errors, precision errors, correctly recognized gestures, and user-reported workload. Findings demonstrate the feasibility, technical reliability, and functional versatility of the proposed platform by providing a physiology-driven framework for immersive motor interaction that is compatible with different EMG acquisition systems and dissociates motor control from the morphology of the controlled virtual effector. Because the two systems were used for different components of the validation, we do not establish equivalence in their performance. By integrating online EMG decoding, VR, and quantitative performance monitoring, the platform offers a tool for future applications in rehabilitation, prosthetic training, and studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging and high-density electroencephalography to address whether training with the platform induces changes in functional brain organization.

piezas.titulo: Effects of resistance training on neuronal response to visual food cues in adults with overweight/obesity.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Individuals with overweight/obesity show altered neuronal response to food cues, but how exercise affects this response remains unclear. This study examined resistance training (RT) effects on neuronal response to visual food cues and eating behaviors in adults with overweight/obesity. We hypothesized RT would be associated with decreased response in brain regions involved in regulating energy intake and decreased ad libitum intake, with brain and behavioral changes correlated. Exploratory analyses evaluated RT effects on eating behaviors and whole-brain response and compared RT with a 12-week diet intervention. Methods Participants (N = 19) completed a visual food cues task during functional magnetic resonance imaging in fasted and fed states, before and after a 12-week RT program. Paired t-tests examined RT effects on response to high-calorie foods versus non-food objects in regions of interest (ROIs; dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula, nucleus accumbens), energy intake, Three Factor Eating Questionnaire, and whole-brain response. Repeated measures correlations examined associations between changes in ROIs and energy intake. Linear mixed models compared RT and diet (N = 17). Results RT was associated with decreased dietary disinhibition (p = 0.009) and increased restraint (p = 0.023). No significant within-group effects were observed on neuronal response, energy intake, or associations between the two. Between-group analyses demonstrated (1) increased restraint across groups (p = 0.017), with a stronger effect for diet, and (2) a significant group*time interaction in right posterior insula and left primary somatosensory cortex (p Conclusions Despite an absence of observed changes in predefined ROIs or energy intake, RT may promote self-regulatory eating behaviors in adults with overweight/obesity. Exploratory analyses suggest RT and diet may have distinct effects on neuronal response to food cues, with RT decreasing and diet increasing response in interoceptive and sensory processing regions. Findings should be interpreted with caution, however, given the small, non-randomized sample. Clinical trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT02047721 and NCT03985787.

piezas.titulo: Sensory Processing Differences in Children With Idiopathic Toe Walking: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceThe cause of idiopathic toe walking (ITW) remains unclear, though impaired sensory processing has often been hypothesized to be linked to ITW.ObjectivesThe objective of this article is to review the literature on toe-walking to identify how sensory processing contributes to ITW.Data SourcesFour databases (CINAHL, Pubmed, PsychINFO, and SCOPUS) were searched for papers related to sensory processing and ITW published prior to July 2024. References of retrieved papers were reviewed for additional sources.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe PRISMA guidelines for scoping review were used to abstract the data following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Inclusion criteria were examined and papers included at least one sensory system related to ITW was studied. Papers were excluded if toe walking was due to diagnosed neurological, orthopedic, or genetic conditions.FindingsOur scoping review identified 13 published articles relevant to examining sensory processing in children with ITW. Studies explored differences in vibration perception, light touch, proprioception, vestibular, visual processing, sensorimotor functional assessments, and parental surveys of sensory processing. Six of the papers were included in a meta-analysis on vibration perception threshold that failed to reach significance ( p = .12). Despite heterogeneity across studies in participants, methods, and outcomes, a meta-analysis for atypical scores from parent-report sensory processing survey data yielded significant differences between children with ITW and typical controls ( p < .0068).Conclusions and RelevanceChildren with ITW demonstrate impairments across multiple domains of sensory processing and sensory-motor function suggesting an underlying relationship between ITW and sensory differences. Children with ITW, however, represent a diverse group of individuals with significant between-subjects variability in which senses are impaired, and which outcome measures best capture these differences.

piezas.titulo: Impaired cholinergic modulation of striatal spiny projection neurons in repetitive behaviors associated with TSHZ3-linked autism spectrum disorder
piezas.resumenOriginal: Alterations in central cholinergic systems are implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We previously identified TSHZ3 as an ASD-linked gene and provided evidence, from transgenic mouse models, supporting the view that striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs) are key players in the core ASD trait represented by repetitive behaviors (RBs). Indeed, conditional deletion of Tshz3 in cholinergic neurons (Chat-cKO model) results in RBs associated with reduced SCIN firing activity and decreased striatal cholinergic tone. Here we tackled the resulting adaptations in the striatal circuitry underlying RBs in Chat-cKO, focusing on the two populations of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) that express dopamine D1 (D1R) or D2 (D2R) receptor. Using patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings, as well as behavioral, pharmacological and molecular approaches, we show reduced cholinergic transmission through the muscarinic M1 receptor onto SPNs, with no changes in the functionality or expression of this receptor. Notably, we demonstrate a loss of the differential excitability of D1R- vs. D2R-SPNs. Finally, acute in vivo treatment with the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil significantly alleviates RBs in mutant mice. These findings point to dysfunction of SCINs as a pathological and druggable mechanism underlying RBs in Tshz3-linked ASD, and to altered SPN excitability as a critical contributor in the resulting pathophysiological functioning of the striatum.

fuente.nota: Ya estaba en el proyecto antes de este catalogo. Preprints sin revision por pares.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de genética: la falta de modulación colinérgica también altera la excitabilidad neuronal. En ratones con eliminación de Tshz3 en interneuronas colinérgicas, se redujo la actividad de los interneuronas estriatales y la transmisión por el receptor M1 en neuronas proyectoras. Donepezilo alivia esos comportamientos repetitivos.

Con la opción WHATSAPP_WEBHOOK_ALLOW habilitada, un atacante remoto no autenticado podría manipular dicho parámetro para alterar la consulta. piezas.titulo: The relationship between gait kinematics and cognitive impairment in Parkinson’s disease
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundGait impairment and cognitive dysfunction are common in Parkinson’s disease (PD), but the interaction between these domains, particularly under dual-task walking, is less well characterised.ObjectiveTo examine associations between gait parameters and cognitive domains in PD during single- and dual-task walking.Methods50 individuals with PD and 21 age-matched healthy controls completed single-task walking and two dual-task conditions, involving naming animals and performing serial subtraction by seven. Gait was recorded using an electronic pressure-sensitive walkway (Zeno™, ProtoKinetics) and analysed for velocity, step length, step time, step length variability, and step time variability. Participants completed cognitive assessments of processing speed, executive function, memory, and language. Associations between gait parameters and cognitive domains were assessed for significant correlations.ResultsIn participants with PD, executive dysfunction, measured by the Trail Making Test Part B (TMT-B), was differentially associated with increased step length variability during dual-task walking. Less robust findings were observed for single-task conditions or other cognitive domains.ConclusionExecutive dysfunction appears to relate to impaired control of gait variability under dual-task conditions in PD, consistent with a key role for attentional-executive resources in maintaining stable gait. These findings may help focus future work on specific dual-task interferences relevant to PD progression and gait decline.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede la dificultad ejecutiva alterar la forma de caminar? piezas.titulo: Validation of the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised in patients with disorders of consciousness
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveOur objective was to validate the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R).DesignWe conducted a multicenter study across neurology, intensive care, neuro-rehabilitation, and nursing departments in Hungary. Thirty-one patients (17 males; mean age 49.1 ± 16.1 years) with disorders of consciousness (DOC) following severe acquired brain injury were assessed. Two independent raters reassessed the same patients within a one-week window to evaluate inter-rater and intra-rater reliability. We assessed reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa and evaluated concurrent validity using Spearman’s rank correlation.ResultsConcurrent validity with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was strong across all raters and time points (rho = 0.882–0.934, p < 0.001). Inter-rater reliability for the total score was excellent at initial assessment (wk = 0.977) and remained high at follow-up (wk = 0.977). Diagnostic classification agreement between raters was nearly perfect (wk = 0.936–1.000).ConclusionThe Hungarian CRS-R is a valid and reliable instrument that preserves the robustness of the original version. Its implementation fills a critical gap in national healthcare by providing an evidence-based tool to reduce DOC misdiagnosis rates.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de fuerza: también de tiempo, pues la versión húngara de la Escala de Recuperación del Coma valida contra la Escala de Glasgow. piezas.titulo: Postnatal Development of Sensory Circuits Supporting Lifelong Social Behaviors.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Sensory systems are essential for young animals as they interact with their environments in order to survive and grow. These environments frequently involve other animals, especially early in life. Thus, animals' social interactions fundamentally shape and are shaped by their sensory circuit development. This Review and its associated Minisymposium will highlight new discoveries centered around the reciprocal relationship between sensory development and social interactions. Points of intersection range from gene expression in peripheral sensors to functional connectivity and neural coding in cortical circuits and span varied sensory systems and species. Taken together, we identify a common theme of refinement and specialization of sensory processing during limited developmental windows for species-relevant social behaviors. Consequently, early disruptions to sensory processing can have significant and long-lasting consequences for animals' lifelong behavior and may even contribute to the etiology of autism and related developmental disorders. Thus, the work presented herein offers mechanistic insight into the complex interplay between early sensory and social development with potentially significant clinical implications. Many of these insights are made possible by technological advances in measuring and manipulating sensory circuit functions and behaviors in developing animals. This Review aims to highlight recent advances and outstanding questions that lie at the nexus of sensory, social, and developmental neuroscience.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. piezas.titulo: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
piezas.resumenOriginal: High-ventilation breathwork (HVB) is a simple breathing technique that nevertheless frequently triggers experiences resembling psychedelic states. While recent studies have begun to pinpoint physiological and neural changes involved in altered states of consciousness (ASCs) evoked by HVB, the interplay between neural and experiential dynamics throughout an HVB session remains unclear. Here we tracked neural activity (via 64-channel EEG recordings) as well as subjective experience depth and content in 25 experienced HVB practitioners across resting-state recordings interleaved throughout a naturalistic HVB session. We find that neural dynamics evoked by HVB emulate the most robust neural signatures of classical psychedelic states, specifically (1) loosening of temporal structure, including broadband cortical desynchronization, increased signal complexity, and decreased oscillatory power in the Alpha (8 - 13 Hz) range, and (2) reorganization of spatial structure, including a flattening of cortical processing hierarchy. These neural effects directly correlated with participants subjective depth with minute resolution, but were not explained by isolated features of HVB such as music listening or active interoception. Together, these results identify unifying neural features of psychedelic-like ASCs regardless of induction method, demonstrating that cortical states triggered by psychedelics can also be accessed by non-pharmacological routes, and breathwork is a powerful way to do so.
