piezas.titulo: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas
piezas.resumenOriginal: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas emcamara 29/10/2026 26/11/2026 Fecha y hora: 26/11/26, 5pm CET Ponentes : Anna-Maria Bucur, Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Università della Svizzera italiana (Italia) Presentador: Paolo Rosso, Universidad Politécnica de Valencia (España). Resumen: La presentación analiza cómo el procesamiento del lenguaje natural puede respaldar la investigación psicológica analizando interacciones procedentes de redes sociales para comprender mejor el malestar psicológico. Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo. piezas.titulo: The role of the right temporal lobe in neural network mechanisms during working memory encoding
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundVisual working memory (vWM) impairment is common in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and is more severe in those with right TLE (RTLE), suggesting the significant role of right temporal lobe in WM processes.MethodsWe recruited patients with left TLE (LTLE group, n = 20), RTLE (RTLE group, n = 20) and 35 healthy controls (Control), and examined their vWM performance while simultaneously recording task-based EEG. The alterations in the neural oscillations and neural network were analyzed during the WM encoding phase. In addition, we examined the relationship between the neural oscillations and WM performance, as well as the relationship between the neural network and WM performance, to further explore the role of the right temporal lobe in WM encoding.ResultsRemarkably lower accuracy (both p < 0.001) and significantly longer response times (LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.026; RTLE vs. Control: p < 0.001) were found in both LTLE and RTLE groups compared with controls. The RTLE group experienced notably delayed response time in comparison to the LTLE group (p = 0.026). In comparison to the LTLE group, the RTLE group displayed reduced theta power spectral density for the frontal (p = 0.024) and occipital (p = 0.011) regions, along with the Fz channel (p = 0.047). DTFF_outflow and DTFFz_outflow values in the RTLE group displayed reduction relative to the LTLE group (DTFF_outflow:p = 0.026; DTFFz_outflow: p = 0.037). The LTLE group showed weakened information flow from Fz to P3 (IFFz → P3, ANOVA, F = 3.45, p = 0.037; LSD, LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.013), whereas the RTLE group exhibited weakened information flow from Fz to P4 (IFFz → P4; ANOVA, F = 3.78, p = 0.028; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.029), Fz to T4 (IFFz → T4; ANOVA, F = 4.67, p = 0.012; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.009), and Fz to TP8 (IFFz → TP8; ANOVA, F = 3.11, p = 0.050; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.017), which were positively associated with accuracy and inversely associated with response time.ConclusionAbnormal information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the superior parietal lobe during the encoding phase may causes WM deficits; damage to information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the right middle temporal and right inferior temporal gyri exacerbates WM impairments.

piezas.titulo: Validity and Reliability of the Activity Card Sort 3 in Persons With Thumb Carpometacarpal Osteoarthritis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceAlthough individuals with thumb carpometacarpal (CMC1) osteoarthritis (OA) commonly experience participation restrictions, participation-focused outcome measures remain underinvestigated, and clinicians primarily rely on assessments of impairments in body structures and functions.ObjectiveTo determine the concurrent validity, test-retest reliability, and precision of the Activity Card Sort 3 (ACS3) in individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA.DesignSingle-cohort observational psychometric study with repeated measures over a 2-week interval.SettingRemote assessments conducted via videoconferencing.ParticipantsThirty-three adults with radiographically confirmed CMC1 OA completed two virtual assessments approximately 2 weeks apart.Outcomes and MeasuresConcurrent validity was examined by comparing ACS3 domain and total scores with the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0). Test-retest reliability of the "current," "previous," and "% retained" activities scores was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1 ). Precision was assessed using the standard error of measurement and minimal detectable change.ResultsThe ACS3 demonstrated good concurrent validity through strong associations with conceptually related WHODAS 2.0 domains. "Current" and "% retained" scores demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability across all domains. "Current" scores consistently showed the highest reliability and precision. "Previous" scores demonstrated lower reliability and greater measurement error, suggesting recall bias. Carrying forward "previous" scores from session 1 to session 2 improved the reliability of "% retained" scores.Conclusions and RelevanceThe ACS3 is a valid and reliable measure of participation for individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA. The "current" and "% retained" scores may support occupational therapy practitioners in conducting participation-focused assessment of persons with CMC1 OA.

piezas.titulo: Somatosensory phenotyping in women with persistent genital arousal disorder: a case-control study.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Introduction Persistent genital arousal disorder (PGAD) is a rare and distressing condition characterized by persistent, unwanted genital arousal in the absence of sexual desire or stimulation. Persistent genital arousal disorder is increasingly recognized as a disorder of abnormal genital sensory processing, but objective neurophysiological data remain limited. Methods We conducted an exploratory case-control study to characterize somatosensory function in women with PGAD. Thirty women with PGAD and 30 age-matched healthy controls were recruited at Leiden University Medical Center. Participants underwent quantitative sensory testing (QST) at hand and external genital sites, conditioned pain modulation, and corneal confocal microscopy. Results Hand QST values were within normal range in both groups. In the genital region, PGAD participants showed altered thermal pain processing, with cold and heat hyperalgesia compared with controls. Mechanical pain thresholds did not differ between groups; however, PGAD participants reported higher pain intensity ratings to mechanical stimuli and showed significantly greater temporal summation of pain in genital regions. Genital dynamic mechanical allodynia occurred more frequently in PGAD participants but did not differ significantly at the group level. Conditioned pain modulation magnitude did not differ between groups and showed substantial interindividual variability. Corneal confocal microscopy abnormalities were observed in a proportion of participants in both groups without significant between-group differences. Discussion These findings show that QST is feasible in women with PGAD and indicate that PGAD is associated with altered somatosensory processing demonstrating genital thermal hypersensitivity and central pain sensitization in a subset of patients.

piezas.titulo: Nucleus reuniens gates selective hippocampal-prefrontal interactions during NREM sleep
piezas.resumenOriginal: Memory consolidation requires functional synchrony between the hippocampus (HC) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The nucleus reuniens (RE) is a structural and functional hub between HC and mPFC. Here, we used in vivo electrophysiology to monitor the hippocampal-thalamic-prefrontal network in rats during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. We identified ripple-like activity in the RE (120 Hz peak frequency, 45 ms oscillatory duration) that occurred most frequently during NREM sleep and was associated with robust recruitment of thalamic neural spiking. RE ripple activity was phase-locked to both hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWR) and mPFC ripples. Although ripples were independently detected in all three structures, we found that coupling between HC and mPFC ripples mainly involved co-occurring RE ripples. These results suggest RE ripples help organize when hippocampal activity engages prefrontal circuits during sleep, with potential implications for network mechanisms of memory consolidation.

piezas.titulo: Increased functional connectivity in glioma: separating compensation from tumor-promoting remodeling
piezas.resumenOriginal: Increased functional connectivity (FC) in glioma is often interpreted as compensatory neuroplasticity or tumor-promoting circuit remodeling, although FC is a measure of coupling rather than a mechanism. We propose a qualitative framework that first examines whether the measurement is suitable for the claim, then evaluates evidence for patient function and tumor behavior separately. The two lines of evidence are combined only when they concern the same patient context, anatomical compartment, metric, and time course. The framework also distinguishes maladaptive or excitability-related remodeling from tumor promotion. Human longitudinal studies associate network restoration with recovery, whereas experimental cancer neuroscience shows that neural activity and neuron-glioma synapses can promote malignant behavior. Increased FC should therefore be reported with its modality, metric, comparator, compartment, disease phase, reliability, and prespecified outcomes before being interpreted as compensatory, maladaptive, or tumor-promoting.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de compensación: el aumento de la conectividad funcional en glioma también puede reflejar remodelación que favorece al tumor. piezas.titulo: How Top-Down Are We? Reconsidering the Gap Between Occupational Therapy's Identity and Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Occupational therapy has spent more than a century defining occupation as its professional core. Yet studies across countries and settings show a recurring gap. Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. This article argues that the profession may face a translation problem more than an identity problem. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Bottom-up methods are not inherently incompatible with occupational therapy; the problem arises when change in a component is treated as sufficient evidence of occupational success. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.

piezas.titulo: MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.15600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

piezas.titulo: Feeding challenges at initiation and maintenance of the ketogenic diet in children with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome: 20 years single center experience.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Rationale Infants with Infantile Epileptic Spasms Syndrome (IESS) are at high risk for feeding challenges such as aspiration. These vulnerabilities may be exacerbated by the ketogenic diet (KD), an accepted second-line therapy. Hormonal therapy (ACTH or oral corticosteroids), the first-line IESS treatment, may transiently enhance appetite and improve oral feeding performance, and hence mask feeding challenges. Methods A retrospective chart review was conducted for infants with IESS who initiated KD between January 2005 and January 2025 at our center. Collected data included ages at diagnosis and KD initiation, comorbidities, clinical and video fluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) assessments, timing relative to hormonal therapy, feeding method before and during KD initiation, and incidence of feeding concerns during KD. Feeding challenges included aspiration, confirmed by VFSS or occupational therapy clinical assessment of feeding (OCTA), or inadequate oral intake. Results Forty infants were enrolled. Twelve (30%) had previous aspiration reported in the medical charts or VFSS at baseline; nine were tube-fed prior to KD. Of the 31 (31/40, 77.5%) orally fed infants at initiation of KD, 23 were referred for feeding safety evaluation. Twelve of these had a feeding concern found on OTCA and/or VFSS, of which 3 presented with aspiration without a protective cough confirmed by VFSS. Nineteen babies were deemed safe to initiate KD orally; however, 5/19 (26%, 95% CI 11.8%-48.7%) went on to experience aspiration or aspiration pneumonia during KD treatment. Conclusion Feeding challenges are frequent, dynamic, and under-recognized in IESS. Comprehensive feeding evaluation at KD initiation and maintenance is essential for safe treatment.

It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Amyloidosis and tauopathy progressively disrupt near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits
piezas.resumenOriginal: Mechanistically distinct neurodegenerative diseases result in similar cognitive deficits, and pathology is often concentrated in a set of circuits known to be selectively vulnerable. Selective vulnerability is an intrinsic property of a circuit: in APP/PS1 mice, where plaques are global, functional disruptions are confined to circuits within the default mode network. What characterizes the dynamics of vulnerable circuits from those of spared circuits is unknown. We asked whether the distinguishing property is the proximity of population dynamics to criticality, a homeostatic set-point of network activity that determines computational capacity. We recorded single units simultaneously in three selectively vulnerable regions (retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and CA1 hippocampus) and in primary visual cortex of freely behaving young and old APP/PS1 and wild-type mice. Firing rate and spike-time variability differed by genotype inconsistently across regions and ages. In contrast, three measures from criticality theory each revealed deficits that emerged only with age and only in the vulnerable regions. No measure detected a progressive change in V1. Avalanche scaling is not fixed in neural activity, but varies along a scaling line as the network state changes. As a result, the lines generated by each genotype revealed a constitutive effect of the transgene in young animals, which inverted with age in amyloid-bearing animals, but only in vulnerable circuits. If the destabilization of near-critical dynamics directly reflects a circuit's functional capacity, the same signature should identify a mechanistically distinct degenerative disease. In a model of tauopathy (P301S/E4), CA1 dynamics were displaced from the control scaling line with the same age-dependent reversal observed in APP/PS1. Our results suggest a network-level principle of neurodegenerative diseases: molecularly unrelated pathologies converge on the loss of near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits.

piezas.titulo: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
piezas.resumenOriginal: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub , we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system. We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted. But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component? References Wickremasinghe G, Sandjaja FR, Rafferty K, Sharma V. piezas.titulo: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
piezas.resumenOriginal: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundWhole person health (WPH) is a multidimensional construct encompassing, physical, and mental health along with relational constructs such as social health that are deeply tied to well-being. Autistic individuals report an overall lower quality of life, but the extent to which these issues are addressed during therapy evaluations has not been examined systematically.MethodologyIn this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we employ a rule-based NLP/lexicon-based approach to examine the areas of focus of therapy evaluations documented by occupational therapy, physical therapy (PT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) professionals. Using electronic health records for children aged 2 to 18 diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (n = 5619 evaluation reports of n = 2021 unique patients), we classified health records based on the domains addressed.ResultsAcross notes, nutrition had the highest average degree of documentation ( M = 2.14), compared to activity ( M = 0.91), followed by wellness ( M = 0.66), and sleep ( M = 0.39). In occupational therapy, wellness was the most common (77.62% of notes), followed by physical activity (76.49% of notes), nutrition management (73.33% of notes), and sleep (34.97% of notes). The overall area under the curve (AUC) from the receiver operating characteristic analysis is 0.89.ConclusionsWhile it is encouraging that most evaluations addressed nutrition or physical activity, the near absence of attention to sleep represents a critical gap in care. Given sleep's foundational role in overall health and daily functioning, its omission is particularly concerning. Occupational therapists and interdisciplinary rehabilitation teams should more deliberately integrate WPH frameworks into their evaluations.

piezas.titulo: Rehabilitation strategies for carpal instability: A scoping review of conservative and postsurgical interventions.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Carpal instability can cause pain, weakness, mechanical symptoms, and long-term disability. Rehabilitation is central to both conservative care and post-surgical recovery, yet clinicians face fragmented evidence. Purpose To map and synthesize rehabilitation strategies for carpal instability across conservative and postsurgical pathways, and to identify gaps that limit evidence-informed practice. Study design Scoping review. Methods JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines were followed. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, with no date restrictions, up to March 16, 2026. Findings were summarized numerically and thematically and interpreted using an ICF-oriented taxonomy. Results Fifty-nine reports published between 1990 and 2025 were included. The literature was methodologically heterogeneous, largely composed of descriptive or secondary designs. Reports addressed conservative rehabilitation, post-surgical rehabilitation, or both, with dissociative (CID) and non-dissociative (CIND) carpal instability being the most frequently addressed patterns. Rehabilitation strategies identified across the included literature were categorized into six categories: immobilization; pain/edema/scar, and education-related management; mobilization; therapeutic exercise; proprioceptive training; and instrumental/physical modalities. Immobilization and therapeutic exercise were the most frequently described components. Rehabilitation strategies varied by instability type, particularly in orthotic selection and muscle recruitment. Pain, function, strength, and range of motion were the most frequently reported outcomes, while participation-level outcomes such as return to work or sport were inconsistently addressed. Dosage, treatment progression criteria, and follow-up were variably reported across studies. Conclusions This review provides a practical synthesis of recurring rehabilitation components across conservative and post-surgical care that may support rehabilitation planning. It also identifies key reporting gaps in intervention content, dosage, progression criteria, outcomes, and follow-up. The findings encourage a broader interpretation of carpal instability as a condition shaped not only by structural injury, but also by the interaction between passive stabilizing structures, active muscular support, motor control, and the capacity to sustain function under load and during activity.

piezas.titulo: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
piezas.resumenOriginal: Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.
